data.title: EasyOPD: An Easy-to-use On-Policy Distillation Framework for Large Language Models
data.author: Jie Sun, Mao Zheng, Mingyang Song, Qiyong Zhong, Gengsheng Li, Zhepei Hong, Chang Wu, Pengfei Liu, Junfeng Fang, Xiang Wang
data.summary: Conventional language-model distillation often relies on fixed teacher-generated data, which may not cover the states encountered by an evolving student policy. On-policy distillation (OPD) instead collects teacher or evaluator supervision on student-generated rollouts. However, existing OPD methods differ substantially in supervision form, tokenizer compatibility, teacher access, and supervision granularity, leading to fragmented implementations that are difficult to reproduce and extend. We present \textsc{EasyOPD}, an on-policy distillation framework built on verl, a distributed reinforcement-learning framework for large language models. \textsc{EasyOPD} separates user-side configuration, method-specific supervision logic, and verl-based execution. Its method modules connect to the shared backend through extension boundaries for loss construction, rollout metadata, reward processing, tokenizer alignment, and teacher-side computation. We instantiate representative methods for three OPD settings -- cross-tokenizer OPD, on-policy self-distillation, and step-wise OPD. Experiments on reasoning, code-generation, scientific-knowledge, and tool-use benchmarks show that these implementations can be executed through the same verl-based backend while retaining their method-specific objectives and task-dependent performance profiles. We release \textsc{EasyOPD} with runnable YAML configurations, documentation, and an installable demonstration package and video.

data.title: Meta-Learning Preferences for Multilingual LLM Alignment
data.author: Jiaying Lin, Seongho Son, Nam Phuong Tran, Long Tran-thanh, Ilija Bogunovic, Debmalya Mandal
data.summary: Unequal availability of human preference data across languages poses a significant challenge for aligning large language models in multilingual settings. To address the lack of sufficient data in low-resource language alignment, we propose a meta-learning framework for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Direct Preference Optimization. By leveraging preference data from other languages, our framework learns a transferable initialization that enables effective adaptation to a target language with minimal data. We provide theoretical guarantees for both the meta-reward modeling and meta-policy optimization settings, and empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on multilingual benchmarks. In an extremely low-resource setting with only 100 target-language preference samples, our approach achieves up to $33.4\%$ win-rate improvements over baseline methods, and consistently outperforms baselines across multiple target languages and model scales. Our approaches retain these advantages across different combinations of meta-training languages and varying linguistic distances from the target languages.

data.title: DV-Lens: Revealing the Functional Organization of Language Model Parameters
data.author: Chenhang Cui, Jian Yu, Jiani Luo, Shuyi Miao, Dingrui Liu, Rui Huang, Xiaohao Liu, Fei Shen, An Zhang, Tat-Seng Chua
data.summary: Understanding parameter functions helps elucidate the internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs). However, how to connect parameters from different modules to verifiable output effects and further characterize the relationship between their functional organization and model capability remains to be explored. To this end, we introduce the downstream vocabulary lens (DV-Lens), a parameter-level interpretability framework that links native parameter directions to their downstream vocabulary responses. Specifically, we first estimate module-specific downstream Jacobians over a reference prompt set for attention query, key, value, and output (Q/K/V/O) projections and feed-forward networks (FFNs). Second, we use these mappings to project native parameter columns into the final vocabulary space, obtaining signed readouts that characterize their average local output responses. Third, we group parameter columns by their vocabulary readouts and introduce downstream vocabulary complexity (DV-Complexity), which quantifies within-group structural variation using normalized reconstruction residuals of the original weights. At the parameter level, randomized controls and finite-difference tests show that DV-Lens readouts capture non-random vocabulary structure and predict local logit changes with 98.0% coordinate-orientation agreement across 720 cases from nine models. These readouts further guide parameter ablation, steering, and swapping across 21 models, shifting target-token probabilities in the predicted directions under controlled conditions. At the model level, the joint-parameter score of DV-Complexity achieves a Spearman correlation of 0.904 with benchmark-based capability rankings across 48 language models. Together, these results provide intervention-based evidence for DV-Lens interpretations and reveal an association between DV-Complexity and model capability.

data.title: AStockArena: Beyond Returns, Can We Entrust Real Capital to the Decisions of Financial Agents?
data.author: Zeyu Liu, Sing Kwong Lai, Xuanzhi Feng, HaoYang Shang, Yang Li, Zihao Fang, Xuan Liu, Song Guo
data.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in dynamic financial trading, yet real-time trading benchmarks mainly evaluate agents by cumulative returns and risk-adjusted performance. Such outcome metrics cannot show whether trades are faithfully reported, supported by available evidence, and consistent with account states. We introduce AStockArena, a real-time decision-auditing benchmark for continuous trading in China's A-share market. Under shared market conditions and execution constraints, we evaluate 13 open- and closed-source models over 3,198 sequential decisions. AStockArena reconstructsthe actions actually posted to accounts by aligning reports, trade requests, execution responses, and account states, and audits them with eight checks spanning execution traceability (O), evidence sufficiency (RK), and financial meta-awareness (B), combining record verification with consensus expert annotation. Of 1,070 trading points, 72.99% exhibit at least one audit gap; model-level rates range from52.2% to 91.2%, with evidence gaps most prevalent. Historical trade-filtering replay further shows thatportfolio outcomes are sensitive to these flagged trades. Decision-process auditing thus offers a verifiable complement to return-based evaluation of financial agents.

data.title: Distinguishing Extraction Failures and Clinical Discordance with LLM Uncertainty on Radiology Reports
data.author: Jerjes Aguirre-Chavez, Shant Malkasian, Roshun Sankaran, Brendan Crabb, Albert Hsiao
data.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to structure data from unstructured text, but extraction errors remain inevitable. We evaluated whether LLM uncertainty could distinguish extraction failure from true clinical discordance. In 5{,}225 vessels from 1{,}045 patients undergoing coronary CT angiography (CCTA) for suspected coronary artery disease (CAD), we evaluated token-level and self-reported LLM uncertainty during extraction of vessel-level stenosis severity. Extraction failure was defined as disagreement between LLM-extracted stenosis and expert annotations. Clinical discordance was defined as disagreement in obstructive CAD status between CCTA and subsequent invasive coronary angiography (ICA). Incremental discrimination was assessed after adjustment for stenosis severity, calcium burden, and coronary vessel. Extraction failure was evaluated in 1{,}077 vessels from 253 patients with expert annotations, and clinical discordance in 1{,}641 vessels from 729 patients undergoing ICA within 90 days. Token-level Stenosis Margin showed the strongest association with extraction failure (adjusted OR, 4.15 [95\% CI, 2.57--6.69]; $P<0.001$) and clinical discordance (adjusted OR, 1.22 [95\% CI, 1.04--1.43]; $P=0.118$). Stenosis Margin significantly improved discrimination of extraction failure ($\Delta$AUC, +0.06 [95\% CI, +0.03 to +0.09]; $P=0.001$), but not clinical discordance ($\Delta$AUC, +0.01 [95\% CI, $-0.00$ to +0.02]; $P=0.245$). In a nested cohort of 138 vessels from 57 patients, 38 of 42 clinically discordant vessels (90\%) were extracted correctly. LLM uncertainty improved identification of extraction failure but not clinical discordance, suggesting that uncertainty may identify errors introduced during data extraction but may not generalize to discordance in underlying clinical data.

data.title: FlashREINFORCE: Critic-Free Single-Rollout Asynchronous RL for Agentic Language Models
data.author: Jian Hu, Yifan Zhang, Hao Zhang, Binfeng Xu, Shaokun Zhang, Hongqing Peng, Zhiding Yu, Pavlo Molchanov, Jan Kautz, Yi Dong
data.summary: Asynchronous reinforcement learning suits long-horizon agents with irregular rollout times, but group-relative updates require repeated rollouts of each prompt. However, group-based sampling limits prompt coverage at a fixed rollout budget and introduces group synchronization barriers. One rollout per prompt avoids these constraints but requires learning from stale, variable-length trajectories without a sibling baseline. We present FlashREINFORCE, to our knowledge the first critic-free single-rollout framework that scales to long asynchronous training and large models. It combines One-Batch REINFORCE, a Sequence Trust Region, and Sample-Mean Optimization, which provide prompt coverage and batch centering while controlling policy drift and length-amplified negative updates. Each component is easy to implement, and the result is their combination: a batch-mean baseline is stable under sample-mean loss, and each common alternative degrades or collapses training. FlashREINFORCE remains stable through 6,000 updates on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B at policy lag four, and through 1,450 on the 30B MoE Qwen3-30B-A3B at lag eight. Under identical loss, data, and lag it matches a strengthened group-relative baseline within 0.5 points, and with half the rollouts exceeds published synchronous baselines on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B (38.0 versus 36.3 five-benchmark mean). On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct it maintains tool use where GRPO stops calling tools and achieves 98.3%/96.5% seen/unseen ALFWorld success.

data.title: Jetriever: Shifting Agent Memory Retrieval from Similarity to Utility
data.author: Ruizhe Li, Licheng Zhang, Mingxuan Du, Zhendong Mao
data.summary: Whether a stored memory helps answer a user's question often depends on world knowledge rather than surface similarity. Jetriever replaces similarity search with full-pool utility scoring: given a query, it uses Jev, an LLM-derived System One decision model, to score every stored memory for the probability that it is useful to the answer, ranking the memory pool directly by those probabilities. On InMind's 125 indirect-query tasks, Jetriever places the gold exchange first in 84.8% of cases (versus 1.6% for BM25 and 0.0% for MiniLM with user-turn indexing) and reaches 76.0% end-to-end Application, compared with at most 16.0% across published retrieval and memory systems. A controlled 20-question comparison disentangles recognizing implicit evidence from ranking it properly: Jev and Qwen3.5-9B both recover 90% of gold exchanges within the top 50 (versus 30% for the BERT-based decision model Laya), yet at rank 1 Jev reaches 85% while Qwen3.5-9B drops to 40%. On a dimension-proportional random sample of 60 MemoryAgentBench questions, Jetriever raises the four-dimension average from 44.3% (ReFind) to 55.4%, at a mean retrieval cost of USD 0.00834 per InMind query and USD 0.03103 per MAB query. Together, these results show that effective utility retrieval hinges on combining broad world knowledge, calibrated ranking probabilities, and affordable full-pool evaluation.

data.title: MultiAgentBench: Evaluating the Collaboration and Competition of LLM agents
data.author: Kunlun Zhu, Hongyi Du, Zhaochen Hong, Xiaocheng Yang, Shuyi Guo, Zhe Wang, Zhenhailong Wang, Cheng Qian, Xiangru Tang, Heng Ji, Jiaxuan You
data.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities as autonomous agents, yet existing benchmarks either focus on single-agent tasks or are confined to narrow domains, failing to capture the dynamics of multi-agent coordination and competition. In this paper, we introduce MultiAgentBench, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate LLM-based multi-agent systems across diverse, interactive scenarios. Our framework measures not only task completion but also the quality of collaboration and competition using novel, milestone-based key performance indicators. Moreover, we evaluate various coordination protocols (including star, chain, tree, and graph topologies) and innovative strategies such as group discussion and cognitive planning. Notably, gpt-4o-mini reaches the average highest task score, graph structure performs the best among coordination protocols in the research scenario, and cognitive planning improves milestone achievement rates by 3%. Code and datasets are public available at https://github.com/MultiagentBench/MARBLE.

data.title: A Survey on Collaborative Mechanisms Between Large and Small Language Models
data.author: Yi Chen, Haiquan Wang, JiaHao Zhao, HaoHao Han
data.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) deliver powerful AI capabilities but face deployment challenges due to high resource costs and latency, whereas Small Language Models (SLMs) offer efficiency and deployability at the cost of reduced performance. Collaboration between LLMs and SLMs emerges as a crucial paradigm to synergistically balance these trade-offs, enabling advanced AI applications, especially on resource-constrained edge devices. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of LLM-SLM collaboration, detailing various interaction mechanisms (pipeline, routing, auxiliary, distillation, fusion), key enabling technologies, and diverse application scenarios driven by on-device needs like low latency, privacy, personalization, and offline operation. While highlighting the significant potential for creating more efficient, adaptable, and accessible AI, we also discuss persistent challenges including system overhead, inter-model consistency, robust task allocation, evaluation complexity, and security/privacy concerns. Future directions point towards more intelligent adaptive frameworks, deeper model fusion, and expansion into multimodal and embodied AI, positioning LLM-SLM collaboration as a key driver for the next generation of practical and ubiquitous artificial intelligence.

data.title: MARBLE: An Agentic Benchmark for Spatial Reasoning and Visual Abstraction
data.author: Yulun Jiang, Na\"el Ouerghemi, Yekun Chai, Maria Brbi\'c, Michael Moor
data.summary: A central challenge for multimodal language models (MLLMs) in real-world tasks is to abstract visual observations into structured spatial states and reason over how those states change under actions over long horizons. Existing multimodal benchmarks often focus on static question answering, where answers can be directly extracted from images, or assume symbolic states are available and bypass the visual-to-spatial abstraction process. We present MARBLE, a diagnostic benchmark for spatially grounded multimodal reasoning and planning across three agent environments: CUBE, MAZE, and BLOX. MARBLE spans 2D and 3D spatial puzzles under geometric constraints, dynamic layouts, and spatial transformations, with difficulty systematically controlled along two axes: observation format and planning horizon. Extensive evaluations show that frontier MLLMs struggle on MARBLE, with the strongest model GPT-5.4 achieving only a 7.3% average success rate across the three environments in the hardest setting. Pairwise ablations on the open-weight models identify visual-to-spatial abstraction as the major bottleneck: when models must infer spatial states from images instead of receiving human-annotated states, success drops from 50.7% to 3.7% for Gemma-4-31B and from 87.9% to 6.5% for Kimi-K2.6. The results indicate that models often fail to construct precise spatial states from visual observations before planning, a task that is straightforward for humans. Overall, MARBLE reveals the gap in reliable visual-to-spatial abstraction for frontier MLLMs and provides a controlled testbed for measuring progress in spatially grounded multimodal reasoning and planning.

data.title: Colosseum: Auditing Collusion in Cooperative Multi-Agent Systems
data.author: Mason Nakamura, Abhinav Kumar, Saswat Das, Sahar Abdelnabi, Saaduddin Mahmud, Ferdinando Fioretto, Shlomo Zilberstein, Eugene Bagdasarian
data.summary: Multi-agent systems, where LLM agents communicate through free-form language, enable sophisticated coordination for solving complex cooperative tasks. This surfaces a unique safety problem when a group of agents forms a coalition and colludes to pursue secondary goals and degrade the joint objective. In this paper, we present Colosseum, a framework for auditing LLM agents' collusive behavior in multi-agent settings. We ground how agents cooperate through a formal multi-agent decision-making framework and measure action-based collusive behavior in actions via regret relative to the cooperative optimum and compare it with communication-based collusive behavior. Colosseum enables audits of LLM agents for collusion under benign settings, different coalition objectives, persuasion tactics, and network topologies. We then introduce a new behavioral probe by creating secret communication channels between agents, showing that most out-of-the-box models exhibit a propensity to collude under this probe, which we term emergent collusion. Furthermore, we discover ``collusion on paper'' when agents plan to collude in text but often pick non-collusive actions. Colosseum provides a new way to audit collusion in cooperative multi-agent systems while presenting observations about how collusion emerges, what affects collusion efficacy, and which strategies may mitigate it.

data.title: Unlocking Continuous Diffusion Language Models via Discrete Stochastic Localization
data.author: Yunshu Wu, Jiayi Cheng, Longxuan Yu, Partha Thakuria, Rob Brekelmans, Evangelos E. Papalexakis, Greg Ver Steeg
data.summary: Continuous diffusion is a natural framework for non-autoregressive generation but has generally lagged behind masked discrete diffusion models (MDMs) on discrete sequence generation. We argue that continuous diffusion can effectively model discrete sequences through the joint design of noise parameterization and token representation geometry. We introduce \emph{Discrete Stochastic Localization} (DSL), a continuous-state framework that combines a stochastic localization channel with unit-sphere token embeddings, resulting in a Bayes-optimal denoiser that depends only on the noisy state, without additional timestep conditioning. A single trained denoising network then supports multiple sampling methods, from continuous denoising to masked diffusion, random-order autoregressive generation and hybrid continuous-then-discrete generation. Parallel generation in this continuous-state framework, therefore, need not imply synchronized denoising: some tokens can establish context earlier while others remain open to refinement. Fine-tuning a pretrained MDLM checkpoint with DSL substantially improves generation quality, as measured by MAUVE, on OpenWebText across all step budgets from $T{=}128$ to $T{=}1024$. The same checkpoint supports random-order autoregressive sampling, and a hybrid continuous-then-discrete sampler using as few as $T=48$ total steps, without distillation or further training.

data.title: How Far Does Online RL Generalize in Mobile GUI Agents? A Controlled Study with AndroidWorld-Generalization
data.author: Li Gu, Zihuan Jiang, Zhixiang Chi, Huan Liu, Ziqiang Wang, Yuanhao Yu, Linqiang Guo, Yang Wang
data.summary: Online reinforcement learning (RL) has advanced mobile GUI agents on AndroidWorld to over 80\% success, but these systems train and evaluate in the same environment, and their training tasks are not released for auditing. How far RL generalizes beyond its training contexts therefore remains unmeasured. We formalize the mobile environment as a Contextual MDP and instantiate a ladder of three progressively distant context shifts as AndroidWorld-Generalization: Unseen Instance, Unseen Template, and Unseen Application, with separation verified manually. In addition, we provide an open RL training system that makes studies at this scale feasible. Applying the identical RL algorithm to two priors of different origin and competence, UI-TARS-7B-SFT at 23.0\% and Qwen3-VL-8B at 52.6\%, we find that RL improves both in distribution but that gains fall monotonically up the ladder (+17.5/+11.1/+4.2 and +10.3/+7.4/+0), with training performance rising throughout while evaluation performance saturates. The decay is algorithm-agnostic, reproduced under PPO, and RL contributes less as the prior strengthens. Few-shot adaptation in the target application recovers +22.9, motivating test-time adaptation as a complement to further RL training. We release the benchmark, training system, recipes, and model weights.

data.title: Training-Free Dynamic Upcycling of Expert Language Models
data.author: Eros Fan\`i, O\u{g}uzhan Ersoy
data.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance on a wide range of specialized tasks, exhibiting strong problem-solving capabilities. However, training these models is prohibitively expensive, and they often lack domain-specific expertise because they rely on general knowledge datasets. Expertise finetuning can address this issue; however, it often leads to overspecialization, and developing a single multi-domain expert remains difficult due to diverging objectives. Furthermore, multitask training is challenging due to interference and catastrophic forgetting. Existing work proposes combining the expertise of dense models within a Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture, although this approach still requires multitask finetuning. To address these issues, we introduce Dynamic Upcycling MoE (DUME), a novel approach that reuses dense experts trained on different domains to construct a unified MoE model. Our method builds a single multitask model that preserves the capabilities of the original dense experts without requiring additional training. DUME is both cost-efficient and scalable: by leveraging the closed-form solution of ridge regression, it eliminates the need for further optimization and enables experts to be added or removed dynamically. Our extensive experiments on different tasks (in causal language modeling and reasoning settings) with several model sizes (between 115M and 9B parameters) and architectures demonstrate that DUME consistently outperforms baseline approaches. In particular, in a reasoning setting, DUME can also surpass the dense expert model's performance in its domain, achieving 104% of the dense expert's performance on average. Finally, we also show that the DUME model can be fine-tuned to further improve performance in complex reasoning scenarios. Our code is available at: github.com/gensyn-ai/dume.

data.title: Sparse Layers are Critical to Scaling Looped Language Models
data.author: Ryan Lee, Jacob Biloki, Edward J. Hu, Jonathan May
data.summary: Looped language models repeat a set of transformer layers through depth, reducing memory costs and providing natural early-exit points at loop boundaries. However, looped models do not scale as favorably as standard transformers with unique layers. We compare standard and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) transformers, with and without looping, and find two main results. First, we find Looped-MoE models scale better than the standard baseline while dense looped models do not. We trace this to routing divergence between loops: in Looped-MoE models, different experts are activated on each pass through the same shared layers, recovering expressivity without additional parameters. Our second finding is that looped models have better compute-quality trade-offs with early exits than standard models. Because each loop ends with the same layers that produce the final output, loop boundaries are superior exit points, as confirmed by earlier output convergence at these points. In sum, we provide a clear direction for scaling looped models: a Looped-MoE model with early exits can not only beat standard transformers at scale, but also enable significant memory and inference savings with minimal degradation in quality.

data.title: When Does Learning to Stop Help? Configuring Risk-Controlled Early Exit for Reasoning-Model Services
data.author: Zhe Dong (University of Maine at Presque Isle), Fang Qin (Stanford University), Manish Shah (Independent Researcher)
data.summary: Early exit lowers the cost of serving a reasoning model by stopping its reasoning once a provisional answer looks final. An operator must choose between a learned stopping rule and one static token budget, and savings against full reasoning do not settle the choice. We present a procedure that decides on calibration data from the workload. It certifies both families with Learn-then-Test to one bound on the fraction of all questions that full reasoning answers correctly but early exit does not, prices provisional answers as the serving stack does, and deploys the cheapest certified candidate. Across four models and five benchmarks neither family is better throughout. At a 5% risk target the learned rule saves 10.4-17.0 percentage points more tokens than the static budget on free-form mathematics with Qwen3, with accuracy 2.4-2.9 points below full reasoning, and less on MMLU-Pro on average. Which family costs less also changes with the risk target, in 8 of 15 settings, and with the price of a provisional answer. Across three prices, committing to one family in advance gives up as much as 27.4 points on some workload, whereas selecting on calibration data falls at most 11.6 points short of the better family, on a task with only 99 calibration questions. In a vLLM engine with Qwen3-8B, mean response time fell in proportion to generated tokens. Policies served on a task other than their calibration task exceeded the risk target in 18 of 44 task pairs; recalibration on the new task restored risk control.

data.title: MOLT: A Hugging Face-Native, Minimal, and Scalable Framework for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
data.author: Jian Hu, Huiying Li, Hao Zhang, Binfeng Xu, Yifan Zhang, Shaokun Zhang, Hemil Desai, Michael Demoret, Pavlo Molchanov, Jan Kautz, Yi Dong
data.summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) research iterates quickly on agents, rewards, and learning algorithms, while policies have grown to hundreds of billions of parameters and beyond. Existing open frameworks force a choice: those that are easy to modify do not scale to the largest models, and those that scale rely on Megatron, which needs dedicated bridge code for every model family and several times more framework code. We present MOLT, an open-source framework built for research that is Hugging Face-native, minimal, and scalable. Its code is easy to modify: the entire RL path is approximately 9.2K lines of Python with one training backend and one rollout engine, so a researcher or an AI coding agent can read it in full and edit the code that actually runs. A Hugging Face checkpoint is loaded directly into a PyTorch FSDP2 trainer with tensor, expert, and context parallelism, so a new model family needs no bridge, and the same code scales from a 4B model to a 753B one. Existing OpenAI- and Anthropic-SDK agents are trained by redirecting their client, with automatic handling of agents that rewrite their own context; training is fully asynchronous; and trajectory data stay in a distributed object store. With MOLT, a 30B mixture-of-experts tool agent trains stably for 1,464 asynchronous updates, a visual computer-use agent improves on OSWorld, asynchronous training is 2.40 times faster than synchronous training, and pipeline throughput reaches 92% of a Megatron-based stack. Its trainer, NeMo AutoModel, trains models of one to 2.8 trillion parameters.

data.title: XMerge: Cross-Axis Selection and Reconstructive Layer Merging for LLM Depth Compression
data.author: Jundong Hu, Shekar Ramachandran
data.summary: Removing complete transformer layers preserves a standard serving architecture, but existing depth-compression methods can lose substantial quality, and the loss varies unpredictably across models. We introduce XMerge, a post-training method with two components. Cross-axis selection identifies a block with low relative-magnitude and angular hidden-state change, and local boundary reconstruction re-fits the adjacent surviving block to match the original two-block output. XMerge uses no task labels or end-to-end fine-tuning, and it introduces neither architectural changes nor additional inference-time parameters. Across seven Llama and Qwen backbones (0.5B-8B), five published baselines, and three layer-reduction levels, its advantage over baselines is largest at the most aggressive removal: at k=4 it ranks first on six of seven backbones on CORE (a 22-task aggregate) and, separately, on six of seven on MMLU (five of seven on both at once), while avoiding the large perplexity increases of several competing operators. In a task-level bootstrap, the 95% confidence intervals for the three largest CORE margins exclude zero; the remaining margins are consistent with ties. Across the 14 (model, regime) cells it is also the only evaluated operator that never collapses, ranking top-2 in both zero-shot and in-context regimes; on a first calibration probe (one backbone) it is the best-calibrated operator. Ablations show that local reconstruction provides most of the gain, while cross-axis fusion helps when the two selection axes disagree. The additional construction cost is recovered through per-token decode savings after roughly tens of thousands of requests.

data.title: Circuit Hypernetworks for Quantum-Augmented Diffusion Language Models
data.author: Xiaoqiang Wang, Mengyang Xiong, Jun Dai, Bang Liu
data.summary: Improving pretrained language models with limited adaptation data calls for computational modules that are both effective and scalable. Parameterized quantum circuits offer expressive transformations for language modeling, yet existing quantum-enhanced language models apply the same predefined circuit design to every token in an input sequence, regardless of its content. This limitation is particularly acute in masked-diffusion language models, where token representations evolve across iterative denoising steps while the circuit design remains fixed. We introduce HyperQ, a quantum-augmented masked-diffusion language model that dynamically synthesizes token-specific quantum circuits. Built upon an IQP-inspired architecture, HyperQ employs a lightweight circuit hypernetwork to generate rotation angles and measurement bases conditioned on each token's hidden state. The resulting quantum expectation values are projected back into the frozen language-model backbone through a residual connection. To support wider quantum registers, HyperQ bounds circuit interaction degree, maintaining per-qubit gradient scale and readout cost independent of register width. Across six zero-shot benchmarks, scaling HyperQ from 16 to 64 qubits improves average accuracy from 47.65 to 54.30, surpassing the frozen backbone's 49.59 by 4.71 points while using only one tenth of the fine-tuning data used by classical baselines. We further execute the generated circuits on an IBM 156-qubit superconducting quantum processor, demonstrating their feasibility on physical quantum hardware.

data.title: LoongSage: A Production-Grade, High-Efficiency Agentic RL Framework for Frontier LLMs with Validated Recipes
data.author: LoongSage Team, Bowei Song, Caiwei Zhao, Chuwen Liu, Dechuang Gu, Dong Fang, Feiyu Xie, Huaiyu Li, Hui Zhang, Jian Tian, Jian Wang, Jie Zhao, Liguang Li, Maoyun Wang, Meiyan Yang, Minghan Zhu, Pai Liu, Pandeng Yao, Renbao Tian, Ru Yang, Shuai Jia, Shuai Tan, Shuailong Li, Shuliang Li, Teng Jin, Tianze Yang, Wenbo Cui, Wenjing Bai, Wenkang Wu, Xiaowei Jiang, Xiaoyi Dong, Yanpeng Wang, Yanwen Wang, Yaohui Ma, Yawen Wang, Yihang Zhang, Yingjie Yan, Zhanbiao Lian, Zhenyu Lu, Zhida Hu, Zhihui Hao, Zhihui Hu, Zhiwen Xiao, Zhiyi Gao, Zhongwei Qi, Zhuangzhuang Wu, Ziqian Liu, Ziyue Zheng
data.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a critical phase in the post-training pipeline of large language models (LLMs). As the frontier of LLM capabilities shifts from static reasoning to agentic tasks--characterized by external tool invocation, multi-turn interactions, and long-horizon decision-making--existing mainstream RL frameworks have grown increasingly unwieldy, raising the overhead of adoption, usage, and debugging. To address these challenges, we present LoongSage, an agent-native, fully asynchronous RL framework with a lightweight core of roughly 14K lines of code. Built upon Megatron for distributed training and SGLang for high-throughput inference, LoongSage centralizes orchestration within a single controller process and encapsulates all GPU-resident components as Ray actors. It introduces AgentFlow, a unified execution paradigm that orchestrates both white-box and black-box agents. For asynchronous execution, it integrates sliding-window strategies that bound trajectory staleness, and employs TransferMesh, a topology-aware synchronization mechanism that routes weights after each step over the fastest transport available to each receiver. Beyond agentic RL, LoongSage incorporates a memory-efficient Teacher Manager that decouples the scaling of teacher models from GPU memory constraints, natively supporting Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation. Extensive evaluations across four complete training runs, spanning complex reinforcement learning and multi-teacher distillation, demonstrate that task rewards improve steadily while the train-inference gap is kept under continuous control, and the fully asynchronous pipeline removes synchronous idle bubbles, sustaining hardware utilization.

data.title: Measuring and Attributing Evidence Sensitivity in Medical Vision-Language Models via Symmetric Counterfactual Controls
data.author: Bhaskar Gurram
data.summary: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) asked closed clinical questions ("Is there a polyp?") can score well by relying on the question rather than the image, and current hallucination benchmarks cannot separate true visual discrimination from editing shortcuts or shifts in the answer threshold. We introduce a Counterfactual Evidence Framework that pairs each lesion erasure with a shape- and tool-matched control edit elsewhere in the image, adds same-site ring controls, restored and partial erasures, degraded views and natural negatives, tests on held-out inpainting tools, separates discrimination (the Evidence Sensitivity Gap, ESG, and AUROC) from the answer threshold, and checks the labels with blinded physician readers and hidden-state probes. Across 507 main-test cases (1,115 views), nine frontier VLMs claim 41.1% to 61.6% of erased lesions (ESG 0.269 to 0.470), whereas MedScope-4B, a Qwen3.5-4B agent trained on automatically built counterfactual trajectories, claims 9.6% (ESG 0.758; p <= 0.001 in all 27 primary comparisons). Physician readers support automated erasure in colonoscopy, where frontier models still claim 45% of erased lesions against 1% for MedScope-4B, but call a finding present on 54.7% of pooled erased reads across all sources, which bounds what unverified erasure can certify. Across 12 pre-registered training or system arms and 270 decision policies screened under a rule fixed in advance, every apparent utility gain comes from shifting the threshold rather than improving held-out discrimination, and probes point to perception as the remaining limit. We also report a 0/48 pneumothorax failure on an external cohort; retraining with pneumothorax patients in every stage finds 53% of pneumothoraxes on new patients without changing the main-test results.

data.title: Training Language Models for Introspective Oversight
data.author: Alex Lin Wang, Linus Yifeng Tang, Dami Choi, Neil Chowdhury
data.summary: Language models increasingly exhibit behaviors that are difficult to detect in transcripts, such as reward hacking, deception, and sycophancy. Asking the assistant follow-up questions about its actions is unreliable, since models are generally not trained to report their own misbehavior. As a result, approaches to oversight typically involve querying external models. These face limitations: external transcript monitoring operates only on visible model outputs, and activation decoders lack full context and are prone to confabulation. We introduce introspective oversight, which trains a new role in the model to answer arbitrary questions about the assistant, rewarding answers that are verified against the assistant's actual behavior. We implement this by adding a separate, third-person observer role that answers these queries, which we can train solely for accuracy and separately from the assistant. On five held-out oversight evaluations, an observer trained on Qwen3.6-27B obtains a mean AUROC of 0.907, outperforming honesty training (0.864), transcript monitoring (0.828), and activation oracles (0.796). We further find that training an observer makes the assistant itself easier to monitor, with every baseline method improving on average when applied to the fine-tuned assistant. These results suggest that training models to answer verifiable questions about themselves is a tractable approach to overseeing unintended behavior.

data.title: Where the Tokens Go: Heat, Entropy and Error in Agentic Coding
data.author: Al\'an Aspuru-Guzik, Varinia Bernales
data.summary: Coding agents are billed by the token, yet software engineering says nothing about what a token actually buys. Here we introduce a theory of software thermodynamics. The theory draws analogues from classical and stochastic thermodynamics, extends them, and applies them to modern agentic coding. We count the tokens an agent generates as its cost and divide that cost into work and heat. The test suite acts as a software Maxwell's daemon that judges every coding change. We test the theory with an analogue of the experiments in which a single molecule is pulled open and let fold again: an agent makes a change to a repository (coding) and then undoes it (uncoding), many times over, and we count the tokens of every model call. The cycle returns the requested edits to where they began, with each direction started from a stored reference tree, and the spread of its cost over repeated cycles defines a software temperature, which rose with the sampling temperature of the model. About 80 per cent of the tokens of a successful run are generated in model calls that leave the requested change where it was, and we call these tokens heat. The free energy of a change, which we estimate by analogy with the equality of Jarzynski, is 14 to 22 per cent of the mean cost of a successful coding run. Coding costs 1.1 to 1.5 times as much as uncoding. The daemon is imperfect: the verdict of a test suite varies with its environment, and a suite that accepts a broken change has a cost in tokens. The practical implication of the proposed theory could be new tools for analysing and optimising coding agents through the lens of thermodynamics.

data.title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Navigation Behavior of Vision-Language Model Agents Reading Emergency CT and MRI Examinations
data.author: Jonathan Lichtle, Aymen Meddeb, Antonin Birot, Ibrahima Niang, Lisa Gastaud, Riyad Hanafi, Sofiane Dujardin, Corentin Selomme, Guillaume Cachard, Aghiles Hamroun, Gr\'egory Kuchcinski, Su Hwan Kim, Bastien Le Guellec
data.summary: Purpose. To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and image navigation behavior of vision-language model (VLM) agents under varying exploration strategies. Materials and Methods. In this retrospective study, six VLMs read 100 emergency CT and MRI examinations published in a public archive (March 2025-August 2026) under four conditions (free navigation, navigation from a key slice, and all slices or key slices in a single request), twice each (4800 runs). Nine radiologists read 30 of those cases. A large language model judge validated against two radiologists graded the answers. Conditions were compared with generalized estimating equations clustered by case. Results. Pooled accuracy was lowest under free navigation (32.6%; 391/1200), followed by navigation from a key slice (37.9%; 455/1200; P = .003), and highest with all slices (42.2%; 506/1200) or key slices (42.5%; 510/1200) in one request (both P < .001). On the 30 cases read by radiologists, freely navigating models were correct in 30.0% of runs (108/360) versus 77.0% for radiologists (208/270; P < .001). Models formed a first hypothesis after a median of 10.8% of the slices and kept it in 63.1% of runs (755/1196); final answers were correct in 12.4% of runs after a wrong first hypothesis (110/885) versus 90.4% after a right one (281/311; P < .001). Median stated confidence in the final answers was 90%, whereas 38.9% of them were correct (1861/4778). Conclusion. Across all exploration strategies, VLM agents remained far less accurate than radiologists. They adopted an early hypothesis and usually kept it, seldom correcting a wrong one.

data.title: LProp: Propagating Latent Uncertainty through Evidence-Conditioned Belief Revision in LLM Agents
data.author: Kaiwen Shi, Zheyuan Zhang, Weixiang Sun, Han Bao, Colby Nelson, Yanfang Ye
data.summary: When LLM agents pass intermediate judgments downstream without uncertainty, later decisions may treat tentative assumptions as facts. Effective uncertainty propagation must preserve information for correction and update inherited beliefs as new evidence arrives. Yet scalar scores omit information needed for revision, while detailed descriptions and reflection incur additional costs. We introduce Latent Uncertainty, a latent-space estimator that preserves uncertainty-relevant information without lengthy descriptions. Building on this, we propose LProp (Latent Uncertainty Propagation), which revises inherited answer distributions using latent representations and new evidence without additional trajectory sampling. We evaluate both methods across multiple-choice, yes/no, open-ended question answering, and mathematical reasoning tasks. Our approach outperforms baselines on most metrics, while LProp achieves the lowest mean inference-token usage in all eight propagation settings. Matched feature ablations further demonstrate that inherited latent content improves error recovery beyond answer probabilities or model capacity alone.

data.title: Receiver-Conditioned Clarification for Multi-Agent Food Assistance
data.author: Kaiwen Shi, Zheyuan Zhang, Changzhi Liu, Han Bao, Yanfang Ye
data.summary: Food insecurity creates a pressing need for guidance that helps households find usable food resources and assess food choices in light of their circumstances. Such guidance must connect eligibility requirements, practical access constraints, and dietary needs rather than return isolated listings or generic nutritional advice. Multi-agent food assistants can coordinate these tasks, with uncertainty indicating when clarification or verification is needed before a recommendation. However, uncertainty can be lost across agent handoffs, allowing tentative interpretations to propagate as facts and obscuring opportunities for correction. Moreover, confidence that a service requirement has been interpreted correctly is not confidence that a recommendation satisfies the user's needs; local confidence cannot simply be reused as downstream reliability. We introduce an inference-time, receiver-conditioned clarification framework that preserves shared premise identities and replays consistent interpretations across dependent agents. Each receiver exposes admissible decisions and remaining evidence obligations, so question relevance reflects both decision changes and missing support. Information questions and user-confirmable fallback adjustments are evaluated together with their anticipated follow-up interactions under shared budgets. This structure connects clarification to jointly supported plans for resource navigation, nutritional reasoning, and supply-side planning.

data.title: ARISE: Practical Self-Evolving Memory for Accurate and Cost-Efficient Enterprise Agents
data.author: Jiangyun Zhang, Zhou Tang, Kristen Surrao, Zhiyu Chen, Albert Guan, Tor Nitayanont, Yupei Zhang, Roopali Singh, Yunkai Xiao, Shreya Pandit, Julia Huang, Shayan Ali Akbar, Erwin Cornejo, Yuan Li, Yi Zhang
data.summary: Enterprise LLM agents operate in dynamic environments where foundation models evolve rapidly, workflows update frequently, and deployments need to satisfy accuracy and cost requirements. We propose ARISE (Agent Refinement through Iterative Self-Evaluation), a practical memory architecture in which the agent's memory evolves from its own failures without updating model weights, tools, or workflow logic. ARISE uses the model itself or a teacher model to attribute the failures and propose corrections. Then, ARISE keeps the corrections as retrievable micro memory, consolidates them into macro rules, and accepts a rule update only if held-out accuracy rises. Across 14 enterprise-workflow domains from SOP-Bench and $\tau^2$-bench using 5 models, ARISE-Teacher, which uses Claude Opus 4.6 for attribution and consolidation, gains 10.9 pp over the baseline on SOP-Bench and 5.8 pp on $\tau^2$-bench. ARISE-Teacher also outperforms GEPA by 4.5 pp on $\tau^2$-bench and 1.4 pp on SOP-Bench. With the deployment model as its own attributor, ARISE-Self still gains 10.0 pp on SOP-Bench. ARISE-Teacher uses 4.0% fewer model calls and 5.2% fewer output tokens at comparable per-task cost (-1.0%).

data.title: RefinementGuard: Counterexample-Directed Semantic Qualification for Hidden Agent-Tool Execution
data.author: Adhyayan Veer Singh, Fanjiang Ye, Yuke Wang
data.summary: Tool runtimes can lower an agent-selected operation into a hidden parallel graph, reducing latency and context while risking semantic mistranslation. We introduce RefinementGuard: translation validation for hidden, effectful agent-tool lowerings, coupled to artifact-bound, fail-closed runtime admission. Qualification compares a candidate graph with an independent reference on isolated state using explicit parent-operation obligations. We evaluate two repository-level contracts, bug localization and patch validation, on controlled repositories. Among 100 activated, non-equivalent development/qualification faults adjudicated by one human, parent-semantic validation rejects 49/100 (operator-cluster bootstrap 95% CI [33.7%, 64.8%]). The objective is selective admission, not maximum mutation rejection: exact equality rejects 100/100 faults but also all 60 valid variants, whereas obligation-based validation accepts 60/60; its 51 residual misses identify concrete specification gaps. On a frozen disjoint input split, the held-out B2-B3 result is localization-only because 21 patch mutants fail structurally; B3 rejects 38/56 localization defects. In a controlled asynchronous-delay regime, the localization serial/guarded median-latency ratio is 4.50x, and hidden execution exposes 74.3% less parent-visible context than visible execution. Patch validation shows no demonstrated speedup; zero-delay runs expose overhead. End-to-end qualification thus detects lower-layer misses while preserving localization's parallelism.

data.title: Evaluating Governed LLM-Driven ML Experimentation: Lifecycle, Provenance, and Failure Metrics
data.author: Dowling Wong
data.summary: Autonomous agents that run ML experiments are usually judged by the best score they reach. That score says nothing about how it was reached: whether the agent stayed within the files it was allowed to edit, whether failed trials were kept or silently dropped, and whether each keep or discard decision can be traced to its evidence. We propose evaluating such systems on their experimental process as well as their outcome, and we build a governed harness that makes this possible. A control plane, not the LLM that proposes changes, owns each trial's lifecycle, checks its edit scope, decides keep or discard, and appends one record per trial to an append-only ledger. Governance metrics such as the invalid-action rate, the repeated-bad rate and provenance completeness are computed from that ledger. Across six ML tasks, from synthetic logistic regression to language-model training, and 1,445 trials, the same contract applied unchanged. The ledger exposed failures that a task score hides: a no-memory arm in which all 120 trials failed, a benchmark adapter whose bounded proposals ran out, and a reset failure that reproducibility hashes revealed, after which the affected campaigns were rerun. In a matched counterfactual, a loop that logs only successful trials left no record of 43 of 50 trials, while the governed ledger recorded all 50. Memory ablations show that memory's effect on repeated bad proposals depends on the task. We release the ledgers of all 1,445 trials, so that every number reported for them can be recomputed.

data.title: Auditable Clinical Support with Decision Agents
data.author: Tiancheng Bao, Riga Wu, Jan Wienhold, Sebastian Billig, Patrick Winnersbach, Hsuan-Chih Chen, Akis Giannoukos, Jiayang Li, Li Shen, Gary Weissman, Eduardo J. Mortani Barbosa Jr, Dyke Ferber, Jakob Nikolas Kather, Christos Davatzikos, Daniel Truhn, Tianyu Han
data.summary: Clinicians reviewing a diagnostic work-up will ask what was considered at each step and why the assessment changed. Agents powered by free text can reach physician-level diagnostic accuracy, but their written reasoning does not always reflect the factors that went into the decision. Here, we present Decision2Care, a decision agent that works up the acutely ill patient without producing any text. A decision model assigns a probability to each permitted EHR action, and fixed rules carry out the most probable one. We evaluated Decision2Care on the records of 546 emergency admissions across 12 diseases. Decision2Care reached a diagnostic accuracy of 86.5%, compared with 86.1% for the MIRA-v2 agent, and required a median of 2.2 s per work-up, compared with 92-100 s. Each work-up tracked which options Decision2Care was considering at each step. In 10 of the 12 diseases, the differential diagnosis changed most at the test on which the guideline bases the diagnosis. Where Decision2Care was most confident after a single work-up, all but four of its diagnoses were correct (98.5%). We traced each of these four errors back to a single imaging report. Three of them were corrected when that report was removed. The same kind of decision was used to select the treatments, and Decision2Care's drug orders were judged guideline-adherent more often than MIRA-v2's. In emergency patients, its prediction of death was comparable to that of three intensivists on the same cases. In five of the eight intensive care cohorts, it exceeded the best of the three 24-h severity scores within 2-6 h of records. Our results show that decision agents can carry out clinical work-ups while recording the options, probabilities, and execution rules behind each action for audit.

data.title: Modeling LLM Reasoning Dynamics with Structural Representations
data.author: Ilia Karpov, Andrey Atamanyuk, Dmitry Ilvovsky, Aleksandr Anokhin, Alex Elizov, Dmitry Zagorulkin, Sergei O. Kuznetsov
data.summary: Language-model reasoning alternates between sustained activities and local operations. We study how this temporal structure predicts continuation and the computation needed to analyze it. T/E/S combines text, local events, and spans of activity. Across reasoning and information-seeking tasks, events and spans improve next-outcome prediction in 70 of 76 evaluation groups for a Transformer and 74 of 76 for Qwen with LoRA. Span duration and preceding events are associated with transitions, and retaining event history across span boundaries improves prediction. We formulate budget-allocation counting and action-conditional continuation queries, prove counting hardness under explicit encodings, and derive conditions for affordable decision certification. In finite-process experiments, bounds that cancel shared continuation mass recover the same optimal actions as full dynamic programming while reducing mean inference CPU time by 77.7%. On 71 held-out HotpotQA and MuSiQue questions, a compact structural observer improves prediction of whether a fixed inference procedure finishes within a CPU allowance: Brier loss falls from 0.0836 to 0.0756. An annotation audit identifies substantial errors in that observer, separating this computational result from semantic validation of its features.

data.title: Continual Tool-Space Extension Learning for Multimodal Agents
data.author: Jinbae Seo, Jungin Park, Hyunsung Jang, Namkoo Ha, Jiyoung Lee, Kwanghoon Sohn
data.summary: Multimodal agents largely rely on generic tools such as cropping, search, and code execution, leaving specialist vision models outside their tool space. However, bringing such a model into an already trained agent is not straightforward. The challenge is to learn each new tool efficiently while retaining the ability to use existing ones. This work proposes COTEX, continual tool-space extension learning, that adds new tools at efficient adapter-level cost. COTEX locates two sets of parameter directions; one triggers a tool call and thereby opens a multi-turn reasoning trajectory, while the other determines which tool is chosen. The adapter of a new tool is restricted to the calling directions that leave earlier tool choices unaffected by orthogonal constraint. We further introduce a protocol that converts specialist models' existing task-specific annotations into verified tool-use trajectories. Experiments on two representative agents and three specialist tools show gains on ten vision-language benchmarks, with at most a 0.3-point drop on existing tools.

data.title: Metrics-in-the-Loop: Complexity Feedback Reshapes Agent-Written Code
data.author: Nicolas Chapados, Jean-Fran\c{c}ois Gagn\'e, Nouha Dziri
data.summary: Coding agents now write whole codebases in long autonomous runs, guided mainly by whether their tests pass. Yet passing tests alone does not reveal accumulating complexity or gaps in test coverage, which then persist as agents extend their own code. We introduce metrics-in-the-loop, an inference-time intervention that gives agents in-flight feedback: cheap, automatically computed code metrics injected into the agent's context during the trajectory. After each code-changing agent turn, we insert short feedback messages naming changed functions whose cyclomatic complexity exceeds a limit (complexity feedback) or changed lines that are skipped by tests (coverage feedback), giving the agent the opportunity to refactor code or strengthen tests before continuing. We run extensive experiments and ablations comparing several interventions across three long-horizon coding benchmarks and four strong models. We find that complexity feedback significantly reduces erosion, a measure of complexity concentration of code, without affecting held-out correctness of the code. Broadly, our experiments investigate a practical form of agent "re-railing", where timely, actionable measurements redirect agents before weaknesses become the foundation they keep building on. As agents scale to codebases with millions of lines, such interventions become critical to sustaining effective development and long-term code maintainability.

data.title: Evidence-Based Credit Assignment for Search-Augmented Language Models
data.author: Wen Wang, Jindong Wang, Jiahua Bao, Tu Yongsiqi, Yihao Liu, Junwei He, Wenkui Fan
data.summary: Reinforcement learning from terminal answer rewards enables search-augmented language models to interleave reasoning and retrieval without step-level annotations, yet outcome supervision assigns identical credit to every search in a trajectory regardless of whether it retrieved useful information. This limitation is especially severe when all sampled rollouts for a question fail, collapsing group-centered outcome advantages to zero even when trajectories gather markedly different evidence. We present Evidence-based Credit Assignment (ECA), which augments terminal outcome rewards with a training-only auxiliary signal measuring how retrieved documents improve the likelihood of a reference answer. Rather than scoring the full dialogue prefix, ECA queries a frozen snapshot of the current policy under an evidence-only prompt containing solely the question and the deduplicated documents observed so far, isolating the utility of retrieved passages from surface variations in generated thoughts or search queries. Within this framework, we compare two return formulations, ECA-Step (which accumulates step-clipped potential increments) and ECA-Horizon (which preserves the telescoping horizon gain in potential), paired with cross-fold group normalization, novelty gating, and search-local token assignment. Across seven Search QA benchmarks, ECA-Horizon improves strict macro exact match over an outcome-only GRPO baseline by 1.03 and 4.80 percentage points on Qwen2.5-3B- and 7B-Instruct, respectively, outperforming both RLOO and GiGPO. Zero-shot evaluation on MultiHop-RAG further demonstrates strong transfer to multi-hop inference queries.

data.title: RoboBuilder: Agentic Robot Co-Design with Real-world Video Feedback in the Loop
data.author: Ghadi Nehme, Dahyun Nam, Akshay Govind Srinivasan, Faez Ahmed
data.summary: Can AI agents design robots that work in the real world? We introduce RoboBuilder, a benchmark in which coding agents co-design a robot's hardware and program from standard parts, motors and a custom 3D-printed part, and every design that passes in simulation is built and tested on a physical course. Simulation alone is not enough: under public part data, none of 15 initial passing designs crossed the real course, so an agent learns the simulator from measurements it requests and videos of real runs. Across four frontier coding agents, ten obstacles at three difficulty levels, 16,427 simulations of 12,774 distinct robots and 135 physical robots built in an estimated 240 hours, agents solve nearly all easy obstacles and invent mechanisms our search baselines do not reach, but falter at harder levels, when one robot must cross every obstacle, and in the real world, where 66% of simulated passes hold across all levels. Closing the loop helps: shown a video of its real failure, an agent redesigns the robot, sometimes correcting its simulator, and removes 72% of level-1 and level-2 failures. RoboBuilder measures progress toward agents that engineer real machines. Project Page: https://ghadinehme.com/robobuilder.github.io/

data.title: MLE Agents: Autonomous ML Engineering in Large-scale Recommendation Systems
data.author: Matthew Li, Albert Liang, Dilip Raj
data.summary: The typical workflow for improving large-scale ranking and recommendation models is slow and tedious: an engineer forms a hypothesis, implements it as a code change, trains a model, and evaluates it both offline and online, often relying on their own intuition and experience along the way. Autonomous LLM agents promise to speed this up by running the loop on their own, but it is still unclear whether they can do this in industry-scale systems rather than on benchmarks or small proxy tasks. We build human-on-the-loop machine learning engineer (MLE) agents that propose, implement, train, and evaluate model changes on large-scale search rankers. Engineers retain control over objective design, search direction, and final-model review. We identify three obstacles that make this industry setting challenging: feedback takes hours per experiment, offline metrics do not always predict online impact, and improvements saturate after the early wins. We address these with parallel training runs, an objective calibrated to match online impact, and careful context engineering. In one campaign, the system ran 1,097 completed candidate experiments and accepted 325, a 29.6\% acceptance rate compared with 15.6\% in the earlier campaign under a different objective and search constraint. Its best model increases search volume by 0.23\% in an A/B test of large scale. Several improvements were architectural changes the team had never tried, drawn from the broader industry and literature, suggesting that MLE agents can explore regions of the design space that human intuition overlooks. We find that the design of the harness around the model matters: intuition suggests that a stronger underlying model is enough, but in our experience, the design of the loop around it is just as critical. More broadly, our work shows that autonomous agents can do real machine-learning engineering in industry-scale systems.

data.title: Vanguard: Knowing When to Trust the Draft in Speculative Vision-Language Agents
data.author: Hanqi Mao, Jiajun Fan, Ruihan Guo, Shuaike Shen, Ziwen Wang, Hui Ren, Xianrui Zhong, Ge Liu
data.summary: Vision-language agents that browse websites, operate phones and act in homes reason before every action, so every step waits for a large model, a latency and cost that stand in the way of deployment. Step-level speculation lets a small model draft each step and calls the large model only on rejected drafts, but its outcome rests on the judge, and a judge that reads only a step's text cannot tell whether the step fits the screen it acts on. We find that a few samples of a small model can contain a correct step about as often as the large model gets the step right, and not always on the same steps: checked against the screen, small drafts can be not only cheaper but better. We present Vanguard, a training-free judge that leaves the draft and target models unchanged: a general decision model, with the screenshot in view, gives each candidate step a probability of being right in one forward pass; the best candidate is kept if it clears a threshold, and otherwise the large model writes the step. On web, mobile and embodied agents, a 2B draft judged by Vanguard is at least as accurate as its 8B target and significantly more accurate on Mind2Web and EB-ALFRED, while the target writes only a minority of the steps; it completes far more closed-loop episodes, and with a 27B target from another family it is both faster and more accurate. Vanguard is the most accurate judge we compare on the agent tasks; it relies on the screenshot on web and mobile tasks, its calibrated threshold transfers to unseen websites, and across model families its gain over the target grows with the draft's pass@4 relative to the target's accuracy. Vanguard composes with token-level speculative decoding and matches trained process reward models on mathematics, turning speculation from a way to save the large model's work into one that can improve on it.

data.title: SCAFFOLD: Toward Warrant-Preserving Evidence Transport for Reusable LLM-Agent Skills
data.author: Nami Cho, Shailja Gupta
data.summary: An agent skill that succeeded yesterday may be executable today without being justified for reuse today. Tests may cover only observable contract clauses, outcome oracles may be absent, evaluations may inherit the same erroneous specification, and permissions or dependencies may change between validation and invocation. We argue that the appropriate unit of prospective trust is a Warranted Reuse Claim (WRC): a defeasible, claim-specific authorization tied to a versioned skill, target context, evidence, assumptions, and identified defeaters. The paper sharpens this position through Warrant-Preserving Evidence Transport (WPET), a proposed discipline for deciding which historical evidence remains admissible after context change. It distinguishes evidence admissibility from truth of the supported safety or effectiveness claim; states a conditional preservation result and its limits; specifies three-valued applicability and asymmetric context-transfer judgments; and illustrates how provenance dependence and policy-invalidating changes alter authorization. We explicitly relate the proposal to assurance cases, contracts, and skill-library maintenance rather than claiming novelty for their ingredients. A falsifiable longitudinal evaluation would compare WRC-guided policies with strong version-aware baselines at matched coverage, utility, and review cost. This paper contributes a formalized problem statement, testable design obligations, and reporting protocol, not an implemented verifier, empirical superiority result, or proof of universal agent safety.

data.title: Space-X: Self-Evolving Spatial Agents Weaving Clues into Evidence Chains
data.author: Zijian Zhang, Wenqing Tian, Qiang Liu, Liang Wang
data.summary: Spatial reasoning connects visual observations, geometric estimates, and linguistic decisions into a coherent derivation. Yet tool-augmented agents often acquire evidence without clear targets, combine outputs under inconsistent object or reference-frame semantics, and misjudge evidence sufficiency. Thus, more tools or calls do not reliably improve reasoning. We introduce Space-X, a spatial-reasoning framework that self-evolves toward complete, continuous evidence-chain construction. An Execution Agent acquires, associates, and judges evidence per problem using role-specific memory. A Control Agent diagnoses evidence-chain breaks from execution traces and jointly revises tools, interfaces, skills, memory organization, and decision rules. This loop co-evolves capability and evidence use: evidence needs guide capability development; usable results guide actions. Across multiple benchmarks, Space-X yields gains with four base models. Relative to baselines, GPT-6-sol improves answer accuracy on ViewSpatial and MMSI by 50.39% and 23.07%, respectively; Gemini-3.8-Flash gains 47.50% and 25.22% on these benchmarks. This provides a unified route from fragmented spatial clues to traceable, derivable answers.

data.title: A Capability Framework for Evaluating Agentic AI Platforms in Regulated Enterprises
data.author: Abbas Raza Ali, Muhammad Ajmal Siddiqui, Moona Zahid
data.summary: Agentic AI platforms-systems in which LLM agents plan, invoke tools, retain memory and coordinate to change the state of enterprise systems-are being procured faster than they can be measured. Public agent benchmarks score models in fixed harnesses; enterprises buy integrated platforms whose orchestration, memory, governance and tooling layers dominate outcomes, and they buy them largely on the strength of vendor demonstrations. We report an industrial evaluation programme ("bakeoff") run by the innovation laboratory of a global bank in which ten platforms-spanning open-source frameworks, proprietary products and hyperscaler ecosystems-were assessed by a cross-functional panel on nine capability dimensions across three financial-services workloads: counterparty credit risk, retrieval-augmented generation and process automation. Scores separate the field into three tiers that are stable under alternative weightings, and surface workload-specific strengths that aggregates hide. A secondary analysis, however, finds Cronbach's alpha = 0.98 across nominally distinct dimensions and rank correlations >= 0.93 with the total for eight of nine: a halo effect indicating that demonstration-based scoring measures presentation as much as capability. From these lessons we propose a gate-then-score evaluation protocol with four layers (capability, execution reliability, governance gates, business value), trace-level reliability metrics estimated over repeated runs, an autonomy-readiness scale and a reproducibility protocol. We state precisely what the present evidence supports, and what a controlled harness must add to turn enterprise platform evaluation from structured judgement into measurement.

data.title: 3D GameDev Arena: Benchmarking Coding Agents That Plan, Build, and Playtest extreme Long-Horizon Browser Games
data.author: Bizhe Bai, Jiliang Jian, Yuqing Yan, Tao Chen, Ying Wen
data.summary: Coding agents now resolve repository issues and generate compact playable games, but whether they can build a large 3D game from scratch remains open. Such games tightly couple mechanics, scenes, assets, and interaction logic, and their quality rests on player enjoyment, which existing benchmarks rarely assess. Thus, we introduce 3D GameDev Arena, a first extreme long-horizon benchmark of 108 from-scratch game-development tasks across 14 genres. Given only a text specification and UI/UX reference images, a fully automated plan--implement--test--repair pipeline builds each task into a self-contained browser game. Runs average $\sim$1,000 LLM calls ; the longest uses 14,407 calls, 2.13B tokens, and 608 assets. Evaluation spans (1) objective code-level functional acceptance against the game specification, (2) agent-based QA and playtesting of 3D presentation and playability, and (3) blind pairwise Bradley-Terry human preference in a public arena. The preliminary findings indicate that long-horizon 3D game development remains far from solved, and code-level correctness alone does not dictate player preference. The public arena is hosted online.

data.title: Learning to Coordinate: LLM-Guided Workflow Evolution for Token-Efficient Red Teaming
data.author: Xiaoyang Xing, Wenyu Dai, Xiaoliang Gong, Asoke K Nandi, Anthony Cohn
data.summary: Automated red teaming is essential for identifying safety failures in large language models (LLMs), but its practical scalability depends on the resources required to discover those failures. Multi-agent systems can combine complementary capabilities, yet repeated planning, redundant exchanges, and ineffective information routing can make their coordination expensive. Moreover, a target model's response indicates the outcome of a test without identifying which collaboration decision should change. We present Learning to Coordinate (L2C), an LLM-guided framework that evolves an executable multi-agent workflow for each red-teaming case. L2C represents agent responsibilities, execution dependencies, and input bindings in a versioned graph, and associates each graph with records of the information actually delivered and produced. A controller trained through supervised fine-tuning integrates these records with target responses, evaluator verdicts, and remaining budget to retain the workflow, refine instructions, restructure collaboration, or lock further editing. This design connects feedback to explicit changes in subsequent execution while allowing a useful organization to continue without repeated controller intervention. The evaluation protocol covers HarmBench with three execution backbones and two target models, together with component ablations, dataset transfer, and evaluator checks. Across the six executor-target configurations, L2C improves ASR over EvoSynth by 1.4 to 4.5 percentage points while reducing mean online tokens by 35.6% to 37.3%. L2C connects adaptive collaboration to the resource requirements of automated security evaluation.

data.title: Beyond Corpus-Driven Imitation: Evolving Musical Mindsets in the Agentic Orchestra via Quantum Reinforcement Learning
data.author: Eduardo Reck Miranda, Moein Fahmideh Vatandoost
data.summary: This paper presents a framework for computer-aided music composition and performance based on quantum reinforcement learning and multi-agent interaction. We introduce the agentic orchestra, where musical agents evolve distinct mindsets through trial-and-error engagement with a musical environment, rather than through training on large datasets. The agents are implemented as parameterised quantum circuits. They evolve distinct compositional behaviours, referred to as mindsets. This enables the exploration of musical decision spaces using quantum superposition and entanglement within a hybrid quantum-classical loop. We present two complementary agent architectures: atomistic agents, which process pitch and rhythm independently, and holistic agents, which handle pitch and duration as unified note events. Mindsets are shaped through musically grounded reward functions, which can be combined and weighted to develop different mindsets across agents. The resulting system positions quantum computing agents less as autonomous composers and more as adaptive musical partners, each developing its own musical personality through interaction rather than imitation. Demonstrations show how agents generalise their learned behaviour to previously unseen material, operating in interactive and offline batch modes using MIDI-encoded music. While quantum computers are still in development, experiments conducted on IBM quantum hardware confirmed that musically meaningful learning is achievable with existing quantum computers. For composers and performers, the agentic orchestra opens new possibilities for emergent, process-oriented musical creativity, offering a scalable foundation for quantum computer-aided music composition as quantum computing technology continues to advance.

data.title: KnowledgeClaw: Towards Agentic Knowledge Engineering via Omnimodal Hypergraphs
data.author: Haoran Luo, Jiapu Wang, Linhao Luo, Luu Anh Tuan
data.summary: Knowledge engineering (KE) turns raw files into a reasoning-ready knowledge base, a task now within reach of LLM agents. KE has progressed from chunk and graph retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to memory agents, agentic KE and multimodal KE. However, a live knowledge base needs omnimodality, a closed-loop lifecycle and multi-granular application at once, yet existing systems meet at most two and no benchmark measures all three. We formalize Omnimodal Knowledge Engineering (OmniKE) and release OmniKE-Bench, six tasks with 1,829 model-free items over 3,960 real files in five modalities. We further propose KnowledgeClaw, an agentic system that builds an omnimodal typed hypergraph, keeps it current with a closed-loop lifecycle agent and routes each query to the granularity it needs. Against 30 baselines, it ranks first on all six tasks with an overall OKE of 55.9, +14.6 over the strongest baseline. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/KnowledgeClaw.

data.title: OpenKAGE: Open-Ended Lifelong Learning in the Open World via Knowledge-Sharing Agent-Group Evolution
data.author: Wenhao Yuan, Longhui Yuan, Zexi Jia, Ningzhe Shi, Jingwei Li, Shipeng Cen, Pengcheng Luo, Jie Zhou, Jinchao Zhang
data.summary: Building autonomous agents that continually explore open worlds and acquire new capabilities through experience is a long-standing aspiration in artificial intelligence. Existing research often pursues lifelong learning within predefined tasks, curricula, or objectives, with self-improvement largely confined to individual agents. We introduce OpenKAGE, an agent-group evolution framework for open-ended lifelong learning. Within this framework, agents autonomously explore open worlds and continually acquire new capabilities by accumulating and reusing knowledge from their own interactions and the experience of others. OpenKAGE builds on two key mechanisms: (1) a two-layer knowledge representation, with a memory layer for situated memories and an experience layer for transferable experience and skills that retains the applicability conditions needed for reuse; and (2) a knowledge-sharing mechanism that semantically consolidates textual experience into a continuously evolving shared knowledge graph, while executable skills are shared verbatim. In Minecraft, OpenKAGE supports open-ended lifelong learning, enabling agent groups to sustain exploration and reach advanced technological milestones. Furthermore, the accumulated knowledge can be transferred to a newly initialized agent group on a different backbone model, improving its survival and exploration progress.

data.title: Benchmarking LLM abilities on postdoc-level natural science problems
data.author: Alina Avanesyan, Alexey Boldyrev, Liqun Deng, Denis Derkach, Mary Godunova, Mikhail Hushchyn, Dmitry Ilvovsky, Irina Knyazeva, Irina Piontkovskaya, Dmitry Polubotko, Fedor Ratnikov, Ekaterina Trofimova, Zhenhe Zhang
data.summary: Scientific problems have no answer key, so evaluating an agent means deciding what counts as a better solution before any agent is run. Existing benchmarks either match a symbolic answer against a key or, where they require executable work, score it by unit tests, by a rubric, or by position on a competition leaderboard. None of these is the criterion by which a field decides that one published method beats another. STEMBench adopts that criterion directly. Each of its twelve research problems in high-energy physics, astrophysics and neuroscience is scored by its own field's figure of merit, and each comes with two measured anchors: a submission that uses no domain knowledge, and an expert reference reproducing a published method, both obtained by running code shipped with the benchmark. The interval between them states how much of a problem is crossed by scientific insight rather than by engineering. Across eight frontier models, task-level wins and domain-level leadership dissociate: a model that wins five of the twelve tasks leads no domain mean. In the high-effort cross-model comparison, at least one model's mean score exceeds the expert anchor on seven of twelve tasks. The remaining five span uncertainty estimation, latent and causal inference, and cross-site clinical classification. Numerical scores and official-submission validity capture different aspects of performance and are reported separately. We release the tasks, graders, anchors and harness.

data.title: Reducing Inference Cost of Coding Agents with Timeout Cascades
data.author: Boxi Zhou, German Sviridov, Dmitrii Ustiugov, Haris Javaid
data.summary:
AI coding agents have become one of the most popular applications of large language models. Yet, agentic AI comes at the cost of a tremendous amount of GPU compute resources, which limits its profitability and its viability at scale. In this paper, we investigate whether smaller, cheaper models can cut this cost without sacrificing accuracy.
We evaluate 36 popular large and small open-weight models released since 2024 on a software engineering benchmark, and find that recent small models are closing the accuracy gap compared to their large counterparts. We investigate the structure of this gap and find that the gap is highly concentrated around hard tasks that small language models fail to solve while achieving remarkably good accuracy for easy and medium complexity tasks. Following this observation, we show that by utilizing a hybrid inference strategy that tries a small model first and escalates to a large one only when needed, we can achieve up to 33% reduction in total GPU-hour costs and 16.4% on all tasks from SWE-bench Verified, without sacrificing accuracy. Strikingly, this simple cascade nearly matches an oracle-style task router, highlighting a practical path for deploying cost-aware coding agents in production without complex learned task routers and with minimal engineering complexity.
